Rewards for Budget-Aware Multi-Turn Agents That Adapt to Arbitrary Test-Time Constraints

Tom A. Lamb    Adam Golinski    Eleonora Gualdoni    Sinead Williamson    Michael Kirchhof Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [
October 20, 2026
Abstract

Large language model agents are often given an inference budget and asked to maximise success within it. A multi-turn agent has to allocate this budget across many environment interactions. An external harness can enforce the budget, but it remains unclear whether the agent itself can learn when and how much to spend. We ask whether agents can learn this allocation across dynamically specified budgets and which rewards best teach this behaviour. We adapt existing length penalties to budget constraints spanning multiple resource types, introduce new reward formulations, and compare eleven objectives in a shared training pipeline. We train Qwen3.5 models at 4B and 9B on AppWorld with budgets over tokens, API calls, and environment steps, and on the BabyAI gridworld with turn budgets. We train a separate policy for each environment and resource type, with each policy trained across budget values. Training with rewards that penalise overspending substantially improves within-budget success and natural compliance over untrained models and over training on task success alone, with agents learning to adapt their resource use to stated budgets and task difficulty. These gains extend to unseen budgets and, zero-shot, to a shifted task distribution and a new benchmark. Reward objectives trade off success within budget and natural compliance. A sigmoid penalty for overspending most often achieves the highest within-budget success at an individual budget, while a fixed negative reward for overspending generally yields the strongest natural compliance. Combining penalties for overspend frequency and magnitude gives the smallest average gap to the best method at each budget. Overall, we show that a single agent can learn to allocate resources across turns and adapt its behaviour to user-specified budgets using budget feedback without external budget-allocation controllers.

1 Introduction

Agents can solve harder tasks by spending more at test time, thinking for longer and taking more actions in an environment (Snell et al., 2024; Guo et al., 2025; Yu et al., 2026). Current frontier agents give users some control over the effort in terms of generated tokens, tool calls, or environment actions (Liu et al., 2025b). To respond to different budgets, an agent needs to adapt its strategy to maximise success under the allowance it receives.

Budget-aware training has largely focused on controlling the cost of a single model generation (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Wen et al., 2025). A multi-turn agent instead shares one budget across many turns, and at each turn the policy has to decide when and how much to spend given what remains (Liu et al., 2025b). This allocation is usually left to external machinery at inference time, including planners, harnesses, or routers, and is not learned by the policy itself (Zhang et al., 2026; Liu et al., 2025b). That machinery adds complexity at inference, and it remains unclear whether the task-performing policy can learn to allocate these resources itself. Different constraints may also call for different behaviour. This leads to our first question. Can we train a multi-turn agent to maximise task success under dynamically specified budgets, across different inference resources?

We study this through reward shaping. In single-generation tasks, length penalties are often subtracted from rewards when an agent exceeds a token limit. Overlong trajectories are still collected, and they can show how to solve a task, which helps most when successes within budget are rare. Some frontier models use linear penalties (Yu et al., 2026; Xu et al., 2026), and others use step functions (Team et al., 2026). Learned budget penalties draw on constrained optimisation (Altman, 2021; Stooke et al., 2020), while cost penalties have also been used to train budget-aware routers (Zhang et al., 2026). It is not clear in advance which objectives best train a single multi-turn policy across dynamically specified budgets and different resource types. This leads to our second question. Which training objectives best teach multi-turn agents to maximise task success while complying with dynamically specified budgets?

To address these two questions, we introduce a framework for training a single policy across dynamically specified episode-level budget values, with a separate policy for each environment and resource type. The policy is told its total and remaining budget in natural language at every turn, so it can learn to allocate resources as the episode goes on. Within this framework, we adapt existing penalised objectives that punish excessive resource use or budget violations to the multi-turn, multi-budget setting and introduce new reward formulations. We then compare these objectives directly to see which ones best teach budget-aware behaviour. We train and evaluate on AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), with budgets on generated tokens, environment interactions, or tool calls. We test generalisation to budgets not seen during training, distribution shift on AppWorld test-challenge, and zero-shot transfer to ASTRA (Xiu et al., 2026). To broaden the evaluation to a different environment and task format, we also train and evaluate on BabyAI (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019), a text-based gridworld.

Our contributions are as follows:

  • •

    We introduce a framework for training and evaluating multi-turn agents across dynamically specified budgets and resource types, with metrics for task success within budget and natural budget compliance.

  • •

    We adapt existing cost-conditioned objectives to the multi-turn, multi-budget setting and introduce new reward formulations, covering hard success gating, continuous cost shaping, and fixed or learned overspend penalties.

  • •

    We show that the strongest budget-shaped objectives improve within-budget success and natural compliance over untrained models and budget-independent task-reward training across token, tool-call, and environment-step budgets. On AppWorld, learned resource allocation responds to the stated budget and task difficulty and generalises to unseen budget values. Under step budgets, improvements persist on test-challenge and under zero-shot transfer to ASTRA. We also evaluate budget-aware behaviour in BabyAI.

  • •

    We identify distinct trade-offs between budget utility, natural compliance, and overspend severity, with no single objective dominating across all criteria. Dual has the smallest average utility gap to the best method at each budget, Sigmoid-Gate most often achieves the highest utility at an individual budget, and Gate-Neg generally achieves the highest natural compliance.

2 Related Work

Token budgets.

On-policy budget-aware training without an external harness has mostly controlled the length of a single model generation, rather than how resources are allocated across a multi-turn episode. Existing methods optimise adherence to token budgets (Aggarwal and Welleck, 2025; Liu et al., 2026; Han et al., 2025) or learn levels of reasoning effort (Arora and Zanette, 2026), largely in mathematical reasoning. In these settings, the model controls resource use within one generation, and tokens are the resource of interest. A multi-turn agent faces a different allocation problem: it must distribute a shared budget across successive generations and environment interactions, deciding how much to spend at each turn to maximise task success. The constrained resource may also be tool calls or environment steps, rather than just tokens.

Wen et al. (2025) trains across a curriculum of token budgets and uses control tokens inserted during decoding to signal the remaining budget. DAPO (Yu et al., 2026) introduces an overspend penalty for a fixed generation-length budget. Kimi K3 (Team et al., 2026) handles several effort levels in agentic domains by training a separate expert for each with step-function reward shaping and then distilling them. We study how to train one policy across dynamically specified episode-level budget values, with separate training for each environment and resource type.

Budget feedback and allocation.

Budget-aware behaviour can also be added without training it into the task-performing policy. Liu et al. (2025b) show that raising a search agent’s tool-call budget does not by itself improve results, while reporting the total and remaining budget to the agent can improve scaling for large models when combined with planning and verification strategies. In our evaluation, the untrained 4B and 9B models struggle to succeed within budget despite receiving total and remaining budget feedback (Figure 3). Other approaches predict how much compute a task requires (Damani et al., 2025) or route between cheaper and more expensive models under a budget (Zhang et al., 2026). Li et al. (2026) search a value tree at inference time on multi-hop question answering and scale node values by the remaining resource ratio, so the search moves from exploration to exploitation as the budget runs down. These methods all handle allocation in planning, harnesses, or routers at inference time. We instead train the task-performing policy to condition its actions on the total and remaining budget, learning to allocate resources effectively across turns.

Constrained decision-making and budgeted MDPs.

Constrained Markov decision processes (Altman, 2021; Achiam et al., 2017, cMDPs;) typically bound expected cumulative cost and can be optimised using Lagrangian relaxation (Stooke et al., 2020). If the constraints are pooled across the training distribution, a policy can break tight budgets and make up for it on generous ones. Budgeted MDPs (Carrara et al., 2019) extend this to families of budgets by conditioning on the remaining budget allowance, and chance-constrained formulations (Geibel and Wysotzki, 2005; Haskell and Jain, 2015; Chow, 2017) bound violation probabilities directly. We carry these formulations over to multi-turn LLM agent training with a separate rate constraint for each budget, so the constrained objective treats every budget separately and does not pool compliance across budgets.

3 Budget-Aware Policy Optimisation

3.1 Preliminaries

We write 𝒫⁡(𝒴)\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{Y}) for the set of probability measures over a set 𝒴\mathcal{Y}, and model a task as a POMDP ℳ=⟨𝒮,𝒜,𝒯,Ω,𝒪,R,γ,μ0⟩\mathcal{M}=\langle\mathcal{S},\mathcal{A},\mathcal{T},\Omega,\mathcal{O},R,\gamma,\mu_{0}\rangle. Here 𝒮\mathcal{S}, 𝒜\mathcal{A} and Ω\Omega are the state, action and observation spaces. The transition and observation kernels are 𝒯:𝒮×𝒜→𝒫⁡(𝒮)\mathcal{T}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}) and 𝒪:𝒮×𝒜→𝒫⁡(Ω)\mathcal{O}:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\to\mathcal{P}(\Omega), with RR the reward, which Section 3.2 specialises to a binary terminal reward, γ∈(0,1]\gamma\in(0,1] the discount factor and μ0∈𝒫⁡(𝒮)\mu_{0}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{S}) the initial state distribution. Tasks x∼p𝒳∈𝒫⁡(𝒳)x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}}\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{X}) are drawn from a distribution over the task set 𝒳\mathcal{X}. At turn tt, the agent receives the observation history ht:=(o1,a1,…,at−1,ot)h_{t}:=(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,a_{t-1},o_{t}), comprising previous actions and the resulting environment observations. Writing ℋ\mathcal{H} for the set of all such histories, the agent acts according to a policy π:𝒳×ℋ→𝒫⁡(𝒜)\pi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{H}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}).

We optimise policies with Dr. GRPO (Liu et al., 2025c), a variant of group relative policy optimisation (GRPO, Shao et al., 2024) that baselines each rollout against its group mean and removes response-length and reward-standard-deviation normalisation (Section 10.6). Removing these normalisers addresses biases that can encourage failed rollouts to grow longer. The practical training pipeline is described in Section 11.6.

3.2 Budget-Augmented POMDP

Budget augmentation.

We augment the task POMDP ℳ\mathcal{M} of Section 3.1 by pairing the environment state sts_{t} with a scalar remaining budget btb_{t}, following the state augmentation used in budgeted MDPs (Carrara et al., 2019). This gives the budget-augmented POMDP (Figure 2) ℳ~=⟨𝒮~,𝒜,𝒯~,Ω~,𝒪~,R,γ,μ~0⟩\tilde{\mathcal{M}}=\langle\tilde{\mathcal{S}},\mathcal{A},\tilde{\mathcal{T}},\tilde{\Omega},\tilde{\mathcal{O}},R,\gamma,\tilde{\mu}_{0}\rangle, with states s~t=(st,bt)\tilde{s}_{t}=(s_{t},b_{t}) and state space 𝒮~:=𝒮×ℝ\tilde{\mathcal{S}}:=\mathcal{S}\times\mathbb{R}. Resource use is measured by a cost map κ:𝒮×𝒜×𝒮→ℝ≥0\kappa:\mathcal{S}\times\mathcal{A}\times\mathcal{S}\to\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}. Each action is the whole string the policy emits at a turn, including thinking tokens. Its step cost is one, its token cost is its length in tokens, and its API-call cost counts the calls actually executed. These raw costs are independent of the remaining budget. We abbreviate the realised transition cost as κ⁡(at)=κ⁡(st,at,st+1)∈ℝ≥0\kappa(a_{t})=\kappa(s_{t},a_{t},s_{t+1})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}. The remaining budget informs the policy’s action selection. After each turn, we subtract the realised cost from the remaining budget:

bt+1=bt−κ⁡(at).b_{t+1}=b_{t}-\kappa(a_{t}). (3.1)

The augmented transition kernel combines the unchanged environment dynamics with this budget update.

𝒯~(st+1,bt+1∣st,bt,at)=𝒯(st+1∣st,at) 1[bt+1=bt−κ(at)].\tilde{\mathcal{T}}\big(s_{t+1},b_{t+1}\mid s_{t},b_{t},a_{t}\big)=\mathcal{T}\big(s_{t+1}\mid s_{t},a_{t}\big)\,\mathbf{1}\big[\,b_{t+1}=b_{t}-\kappa(a_{t})\,\big]. (3.2)

Budget-conditioned policy.

The initial budget B0∈ℝ>0B_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} and the remaining budget btb_{t} are written into the text of the observations the agent sees (Section 11.5). At the next turn, the augmented observation is o~t+1=(ot+1,bt+1)∈Ω~:=Ω×ℝ\tilde{o}_{t+1}=(o_{t+1},b_{t+1})\in\tilde{\Omega}:=\Omega\times\mathbb{R}, where bt+1b_{t+1} is given by Equation 3.1. The observation kernel preserves the task observation and reveals the updated budget exactly.

𝒪~(ot+1,b∣st+1,bt+1,at)=𝒪(ot+1∣st+1,at) 1[b=bt+1].\tilde{\mathcal{O}}\big(o_{t+1},b\mid s_{t+1},b_{t+1},a_{t}\big)=\mathcal{O}\big(o_{t+1}\mid s_{t+1},a_{t}\big)\,\mathbf{1}\big[\,b=b_{t+1}\,\big]. (3.3)

An augmented history splits into the history hth_{t} of ℳ\mathcal{M} and the observed budgets, so the budget-conditioned policy

π(⋅∣x,ht,bt,B0)∈𝒫(𝒜),π:𝒳×ℋ×ℝ×ℝ>0→𝒫(𝒜),\pi(\cdot\mid x,h_{t},b_{t},B_{0})\in\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}),\qquad\pi:\mathcal{X}\times\mathcal{H}\times\mathbb{R}\times\mathbb{R}_{>0}\to\mathcal{P}(\mathcal{A}), (3.4)

Episode termination.

Each episode draws a task x∼p𝒳x\!\sim\!p_{\mathcal{X}} and, independently of it, a budget B0∼pBB_{0}\!\sim\!p_{B} from the budget prior defined below, initialising the episode at b1=B0b_{1}\!=\!B_{0} with the opening observation o1o_{1} the prompt stating the task and its budget (see Section 11.5 for the prompts in full). Most methods allow bt<0b_{t}\!<\!0, so the agent can overspend and learn from doing so, possibly with a penalty. Reward and budget penalties.

We score the completed trajectory ζ:=(o1,a1,…,oτ,aτ,oτ+1)\zeta:=(o_{1},a_{1},\dots,o_{\tau},a_{\tau},o_{\tau+1}) by a binary task reward R⁡(ζ)∈{0,1}R(\zeta)\in\{0,1\} and transform it into a budget-conditioned return R~​(ζ,B0)∈ℝ\tilde{R}(\zeta,B_{0})\in\mathbb{R}. The agent is trained to maximise the expected shaped return

maxπ∈Π𝔼x∼p𝒳,B0∼pB,ζ∼π(⋅∣x,B0)​[R~​(ζ,B0)].\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \ \mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}},\ B_{0}\sim p_{B},\zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,B_{0})\end{subarray}}\!\big[\,\tilde{R}(\zeta,B_{0})\,\big]\,. (3.5)

We do not discount, so any pressure to finish early comes from the budget and any overspending shaping or penalties. We fix a finite set of M∈ℤ>0M\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} training budgets ℬ={b(1)<⋯<b(M)}⊂ℝ>0\mathcal{B}=\{b^{(1)}<\dots<b^{(M)}\}\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0} and draw budgets uniformly at random during training. Rewards are shaped as a function of this spend as a fraction of the prompted budget B0B_{0}, the normalised cost

C¯​(ζ,B0):=C⁡(ζ)B0=1B0​∑t≤τκ⁡(at)∈ℝ≥0,\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0}):=\frac{C(\zeta)}{B_{0}}=\frac{1}{B_{0}}\sum_{t\leq\tau}\kappa(a_{t})\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}, (3.6)

with C¯≤1\bar{C}\leq 1 within budget and C¯>1\bar{C}>1 over budget.

3.3 Cost-Conditioned Rewards

We compare existing reward objectives and new formulations motivated by heuristics, common practice, or constrained optimisation. We organise them into four groups: (a) hard boundary mechanisms that act at the budget limit, (b) within-budget cost pressure that penalises resource use before the limit, (c) gradual post-budget shaping that penalises the amount of overspend, and (d) learned per-budget violation prices that adapt penalties to the overspend rate at each training budget. The objectives also differ in whether overspending can produce negative returns. Figure 1 and Section 8 give their mathematical definitions and further details.

Hard boundary mechanisms.

At the budget, these methods either stop the rollout or assign a fixed outcome to a violation.

  • •

    Trunc (Liu et al., 2025a) is a baseline that does not permit any overspending. Every rollout is terminated at B0B_{0}, and the reward is the binary task reward obtained within B0B_{0}.

  • •

    Gate relaxes this constraint. The policy may overspend, but any rollout that exceeds B0B_{0} receives zero reward regardless of task success. This provides a simple objective that rewards only success within budget.

  • •

    Gate-Neg (Team et al., 2026) assigns a reward of −1-1 whenever the policy exceeds B0B_{0}, regardless of task success. Unlike Gate, it therefore prefers a failure within budget to a failure over budget.

Within-budget cost pressure.

These methods begin penalising cost before the budget is exhausted.

  • •

    Sigmoid smooths the hard overspend indicator that Rate and Dual apply as a step into a symmetric sigmoid penalty, which applies pressure to solve successfully within budget from the start of a policy’s rollout.

  • •

    Linear-Cost (Xu et al., 2026) penalises cost linearly from the first action onwards, so the pressure starts well before the budget is reached.

Gradual post-budget shaping.

These methods preserve the full in-budget return, then change it continuously with the amount of overspend.

  • •

    Sigmoid-Gate subtracts a sigmoid-shaped penalty only after B0B_{0}. It leaves the in-budget return unchanged and continuously lowers the return of both successes and failures as overspend grows. Unlike Gate, it can assign negative returns to overspending failures.

  • •

    Linear-Mag has no step at B0B_{0} and instead reduces the reward linearly beyond it. It was popularised by DAPO (Yu et al., 2026), and we generalise it to multiple budgets in Section 9.

  • •

    Exp-Mag decays a successful trajectory’s reward exponentially in how far it overspends. Failures always receive a reward of 00, regardless of spend.

Learned per-budget violation prices.

These methods learn an overspend price separately at each budget.

  • •

    Rate tracks the overspend rate at each budget and applies a larger penalty the more often the policy exceeds that budget. We derive it from a Lagrangian perspective in Section 8. Its price is capped at 1.01.0, so an overspending success never scores below a compliant failure.

  • •

    Dual combines a step penalty with a linear one. A learned Lagrangian step penalty prices how often rollouts at the given budget overspend, and a linear penalty prices how much the current rollout overspends. Each term subtracts at most 0.50.5. We study the dual optimisation in Section 10.7 and why the two penalties are complementary in Section 10.5.

4 Experiments

We first test whether a single policy can learn to adapt across dynamically specified budget values, including values unseen during training (Section 4.1). We then compare which reward objectives best teach success within budget and natural compliance (Section 4.2). Finally, we test whether the learned behaviour persists under an AppWorld task-distribution shift and transfers to ASTRA without retraining (Section 4.3).

Experimental setup.

We train 4B and 9B Qwen3.5 models (Qwen Team, 2026) from their post-trained checkpoints (Section 11.6). All trained methods use the same Dr. GRPO pipeline (Liu et al., 2025c), prompts, budget grids, and seed within each setting. They differ in the training return, and Trunc additionally stops training rollouts at the budget boundary. We compare against Base, the untrained model, and GRPO-Std, which is trained with the binary task reward RR alone. Like the budget-aware methods, GRPO-Std receives budget information in its prompt during training and evaluation, but its reward is independent of the budget and its rollouts are not cut off at the budget, unlike Trunc. This baseline represents task-reward-only agent training, without a budget-dependent return.

We train and evaluate on AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024), an interactive coding-agent benchmark where agents complete requests by writing Python over multiple turns. We evaluate on held-out test-normal tasks, the distribution-shifted test-challenge split, and ASTRA (Xiu et al., 2026), an out-of-domain personal-assistant benchmark. We also evaluate on BabyAI (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019), a text-based gridworld with tasks distinct from code generation (Section 11). Across these settings, we consider budgets over steps (agent turns), tool calls (API calls), and tokens (all generated tokens, including reasoning), as defined by the cost map κ\kappa.

At each budget bb, we measure budget utility 𝒰⁡(b)\mathcal{U}(b), the probability of solving a task within budget, and compliance Comp⁡(b)\mathrm{Comp}(b), the probability that the agent terminates within budget when rollouts are not cut off:

𝒰(b):=𝔼x∼p𝒳test,ζ∼π(⋅∣x,b)[R(ζ)[C¯(ζ,b)≤1]],\displaystyle\mathcal{U}(b):=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}},\zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,b)}\!\left[R(\zeta)\,\mathbf{1}\!\left[\bar{C}(\zeta,b)\leq 1\right]\right], (4.1)
Comp(b):=ℙx∼p𝒳test,ζ∼π(⋅∣x,b)(C¯(ζ,b)≤1),\displaystyle\mathrm{Comp}(b):=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}},\zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,b)}\!\left(\bar{C}(\zeta,b)\leq 1\right), (4.2)

where expectations are over held-out tasks 𝒳test\mathcal{X}_{\mathrm{test}}. Budget utility counts a success only if the rollout finishes successfully within budget, matching the practical setting in which the agent is cut off at the budget limit. Natural compliance measures whether the rollout finishes within budget regardless of task success, without an external budget cutoff.

4.1 Agents Learn to Adapt Across Dynamically Specified Budgets

We first test our first question: whether agents can learn to succeed within dynamically specified budgets and adapt their resource use to the task and available allowance.

Budget-shaped returns improve success within budget and compliance.

Figure 3 reports budget utility and natural compliance for Base, GRPO-Std, and the budget-shaped objectives across both model scales, AppWorld’s step, token, and API-call budgets, and BabyAI turn budgets. Despite receiving the same budget information as other methods, Base, the Qwen3.5 checkpoints before our additional training, show poor success within budget and compliance. At a step budget of B=36B=36, the 9B and 4B Base models reach only 37%37\% and 19%19\% budget utility, respectively, while the 9B Base model complies on fewer than half of episodes across the token-budget range. GRPO-Std improves on Base through standard agent post-training, but its budget-independent return still gives weak compliance and lower budget utility than the leading budget-shaped objectives.

The stronger budget-shaped objectives improve both metrics over these baselines, although not every reward improves on GRPO-Std in every setting. Thus, before looking into differences between the reward functions (which we do in the next section), we can record that budget-shaped post-training, using budget feedback without an external budget-allocation controller, can teach a single agent to use its total and remaining budget to improve success within budget and natural compliance across dynamically specified step, token, and API-call budgets. The BabyAI results show the same overall trends under turn budgets in an environment distinct from AppWorld. At larger budgets, the utility curves of the stronger objectives often converge, indicating that these policies maintain similar task utility once the budget is no longer as binding. No method attains perfect natural compliance across every budget and setting. The objectives yield different trade-offs between success within budget and natural compliance. We compare them in Section 4.2.

Resource use varies with task difficulty and the stated budget.

Figure 4(a) shows the mean spend of the 9B AppWorld policies by task difficulty. GRPO-Std spends comparatively uniformly across stated budgets, despite changing its spend with task difficulty. Across the budget-shaped policies, step and token spend generally increase with the stated budget allowance and with task difficulty, most clearly for hard tasks. Under API-call budgets, spend rises sharply with task difficulty but changes comparatively little with the stated allowance, indicating that call use is driven more strongly by task difficulty. Examples from BabyAI and AppWorld in Section 12.4 also show explicit budget planning and action batching in the policies’ reasoning.

Table 1 shows that budget-aware training helps agents use the prompt’s guidance to batch API calls (Section 11.5). All methods receive this guidance, but GRPO-Std uses around one API call per turn across budgets. In contrast, Gate, Sigmoid-Gate, and Dual use around 1.91.9 calls per turn at B=10B=10, compared with around 1.51.5 to 1.61.6 at B=32B=32. These averages include successful and failed rollouts completed within budget. The budget-aware policies batch more calls and increase batching under tighter step budgets. Together with their improved within-budget success and natural compliance, these results suggest that the policies learn to use batching as part of allocating their available steps more effectively.

Budget-aware behaviour generalises beyond the training budgets.

The dashed vertical lines in Figure 3 mark the six budgets used during training. On AppWorld, the step and API-call evaluations include both interpolated budgets between these lines and extrapolated budgets outside the training grid. The stronger budget-aware policies retain improved budget utility and compliance at these unseen values.

4.2 Which Rewards Best Teach Budget-Aware Behaviour?

We now address our second research question by comparing how reward objectives balance success within budget and natural compliance.

Utility rankings of budget-shaped rewards.

Table 2 aggregates budget utility across the eight AppWorld and BabyAI experiments. Near-best rate measures how often a method is within two percentage points of the best budget utility at each budget, while mean regret is the average gap to the best observed budget utility at each budget, measured in percentage points. Sigmoid-Gate most often attains the highest utility at an individual budget, with a 20.1%20.1\% win rate. Gate has the highest near-best rate at 39.8%39.8\%. Dual has the lowest observed mean regret at 2.922.92 percentage points, followed by Gate at 3.333.33, Linear-Cost at 3.753.75, and Sigmoid-Gate at 3.823.82. Thus, Sigmoid-Gate wins most often at an individual budget and Dual has the smallest observed average loss to the best method across the evaluation. Gate performs surprisingly well for a simple objective that rewards only within-budget success and adds no explicit overspend penalty.

Allowing training rollouts beyond the budget improves pooled utility.

Table 2 shows that Gate surpasses Trunc on all three pooled utility metrics, with a higher win rate and near-best rate and a lower mean regret. Gate permits an overspending rollout to finish and assigns it zero return. Tokens generated after the budget boundary remain in the rollout and contribute to training. When the same group contains a positive-return rollout, the overspending rollout receives a negative advantage, providing a learning signal on its actions, including those beyond the budget. Trunc instead ends the rollout at the budget boundary, removing these post-budget tokens from training. The comparison supports retaining overspending trajectories even when they receive no success reward. Note, however, that Trunc has a higher throughput due to not having to generate the additional over budget steps.

Penalty design affects success, compliance, and their trade-off.

Gate-Neg assigns every overspent trajectory a reward of −1-1, ranking an in-budget failure above any overspent result. In Figure 3, Gate-Neg generally attains high natural compliance, but its mean regret is 6.006.00 percentage points, compared with 3.333.33 for Gate in Table 2. The strong overspend penalty may make the policy more hesitant near the budget boundary, sacrificing some success within budget to avoid a violation.

Rate alone is less competitive than Dual, with mean regrets of 7.467.46 and 2.922.92 percentage points, respectively. This is consistent with a learned price on the overspend event being more useful when combined with information about the overspend size. Linear-Cost and Sigmoid, which apply cost pressure before the budget boundary, have mean regrets of 3.753.75 and 4.314.31 percentage points, respectively. These results suggest that early pressure to finish does not necessarily improve within-budget utility.

Small overruns without magnitude penalties.

Even a policy with high natural compliance can substantially overspend on the episodes where it violates the budget. We therefore also examine conditional excess spend in Figure 4(b), that is, in rollouts that do overspend, how much do they overspend in percent compared to the prompted budget. Gate and Gate-Neg generally have comparatively small conditional overruns, despite neither applying a penalty that grows with overspend magnitude. Explicit magnitude penalties are therefore not necessary to obtain comparatively small overruns in these experiments.

Raw task success generally increases with spend.

This paper so far focussed on the evaluation setup where the agent is cut off at the budget in each task. We may, however, also be interested in the tradeoff between how much compute is used overall versus how many tasks are solved. Figure 5 reports pass@1 against mean spend, counting successes regardless of whether the rollout finishes within budget. At both model scales, greater spending is generally associated with higher overall success across steps, tokens, and API calls. This complements the earlier evidence of budget-responsive resource use by showing that spending differences are also accompanied by differences in overall task success.

4.3 Budget-Aware Behaviour Generalises Beyond the Training Distribution

Budget-aware behaviour persists on shifted AppWorld tasks.

We next test whether policies trained to condition on the budget remain responsive to it under distribution shift. Figure 6 (top) evaluates the AppWorld-trained policies on test-challenge, which includes unseen apps and more difficult tasks. As on test-normal, the stronger budget-shaped objectives generally achieve higher budget utility and natural compliance than Base and GRPO-Std at both model scales. Utility rises with the stated step budget and, for the 9B model, continues to increase beyond the largest training budget of 2929. These results suggest that both the learned budgeting behaviour and the gains over budget-independent training methods extend to shifted tasks. Gate-Neg once again generally achieves the highest compliance, while utility rankings vary with the budget and model scale.

Budget-aware behaviour transfers zero-shot to ASTRA.

We also test zero-shot generalization to a new environment. Figure 6 (bottom) evaluates the same policies on ASTRA without retraining. As on test-challenge, the stronger budget-shaped objectives generally retain higher budget utility and natural compliance than Base and GRPO-Std. At both model scales, utility increases over tighter step budgets before flattening at looser budgets, while natural compliance also increases with the allowance. Gate-Neg remains among the most compliant methods, and several objectives achieve similar utility at looser budgets. These results suggest that budget responsiveness and the improvements over the baselines transfer to ASTRA’s distinct personal-assistant tasks and tool domain, using the same Python-REPL action interface (Section 11.2).

5 Conclusion

Simply prompting an agent with an inference budget is not enough to make it adhere to that budget or succeed within it. Without consequences for overspending during training, agents frequently exceed the stated allowance. Budget-aware reward objectives provide a simple remedy, teaching a single policy to adapt its resource use across tasks and budget values. We show that this behaviour extends to unseen budgets, persists under a shifted task distribution, and transfers zero-shot to a separate environment. The choice of objective determines the resulting trade-off. Dual is most consistently close to the best method across budgets, Sigmoid-Gate most often yields the highest within-budget success, and Gate-Neg yields the strongest natural compliance. All three are competitive and require no external budget-allocation controller. We encourage practitioners to experiment with these objectives to select the balance between task success and natural budget adherence that best fits their application.

All tool-use experiments in this work are conducted in research-only simulated environments.
