6 Notation

Table 3 acts as a reference for the notation used throughout the paper, grouped by where they are introduced.

7 Limitations and Future Work

Each policy currently manages one resource type at a time. Extending the framework to jointly manage several resources would allow an agent to balance constraints such as tokens, tool calls, and environment steps within the same episode. Although the remaining budget is updated after every turn, the total budget and resource definition are fixed at the start of the episode. Future work could consider budgets that are revised during execution or costs that change with the environment state. The framework could also incorporate stochastic costs such as latency or monetary spend and be combined with inference-time allocation methods that build on the budget awareness already internalised by the policy.

Our evidence covers two scales of one model family and simulated environments. Most method comparisons use one training seed; the additional seeds cover two objectives in one AppWorld setting and do not establish a reliable ordering among all leading methods. Unseen-budget evaluation covers AppWorld interpolation for all three resources and extrapolation for steps and API calls; BabyAI is evaluated only at trained budgets. ASTRA transfer uses step budgets and an action interface aligned with AppWorld.

Natural compliance is imperfect, and the capped multiplier updates do not guarantee the target violation rate. A strict deployment budget therefore still requires a cutoff. Our prompts provide remaining-budget feedback and resource-specific advice, including instructions to batch actions. Without ablations of these prompt components, the experiments establish the behaviour of the combined prompting and training procedure, rather than the separate contribution of each component.

8 Budget-Conditioned Rewards in Full

This appendix defines every reward of Figure 1 and derives the per-budget price of Rate and Dual. All rewards are written using normalised cost C¯=C¯​(ζ,B0)\bar{C}=\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0}) of Equation 3.6, so that the budget sits at C¯=1\bar{C}=1 and allows a generalised application across budget types.

Hard gates and fixed penalties.

  • •

    Trunc enforces the budget in the environment. It halts the episode before executing any action that would overdraw the budget, at τB0:=min⁡(τ,inf{t≥1:bt−κ⁡(at)<0}−1)\tau_{B_{0}}:=\min\big(\tau,\ \inf\{t\geq 1:b_{t}-\kappa(a_{t})<0\}-1\big), and scores the truncated trajectory by the task reward alone, R~trunc​(ζ,B0):=R⁡(ζ≤τB0)\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{trunc}}(\zeta,B_{0}):=R(\zeta_{\leq\tau_{B_{0}}}). Every training trajectory then complies by construction, but the policy receives no training on continuations beyond the budget boundary. Compliance during training is therefore not evidence that it has learned to stop without a cutoff.

  • •

    Gate lets the rollout continue past the budget but withholds the task reward from any overspending trajectory, R~gate(ζ,B0):=R 1[C¯≤1]\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{gate}}(\zeta,B_{0}):=R\,\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}\leq 1].

  • •

    Gate-Neg (Team et al., 2026) extends Gate with a fixed penalty for overspending, R 1[C¯≤1]−𝟏[C¯>1]R\,\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}\leq 1]-\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}>1].

  • •

    Linear-Cost (Xu et al., 2026) penalises cost linearly from the first action, R−min⁡(1,C¯/2)R-\min(1,\bar{C}/2), so it applies pressure before the budget is reached.

Continuous cost shaping.

Sigmoid-Gate and Sigmoid use the logistic sigmoid σ⁡(x):=(1+e−x)−1\sigma(x):=(1+e^{-x})^{-1} to supply continuous cost feedback. They differ in whether that feedback starts only after the budget or also acts within it.

  • •

    Sigmoid-Gate has return R+1−2​σ​(2​(C¯−1)+)R+1-2\sigma\big(2(\bar{C}-1)_{+}\big). Its additive penalty is zero for C¯≤1\bar{C}\leq 1 and increases continuously towards 11 beyond the budget. Thus, overspending successes approach return 00 and overspending failures approach −1-1. Despite its name, this is not a multiplicative smoothing of Gate’s success gate; the positive-part operation also introduces a kink at the budget.

  • •

    Sigmoid smooths the overspend indicator 𝟏[C¯>1]\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}>1] that Rate and Dual apply as a hard step, R−σ​(2​(C¯−1))R-\sigma\big(2(\bar{C}-1)\big). Unlike Sigmoid-Gate, this penalty also acts within budget, with a slope that varies with cost.

Magnitude shaping.

We adapt the DAPO shaping Equation 9.1 to the normalised cost so that one form covers every budget in every cost unit,

PDAPO​(ζ,B0):=α​clip⁡(C¯​(ζ,B0)−1, 0, 1),P_{\mathrm{DAPO}}(\zeta,B_{0}):=\alpha\operatorname{clip}\!\big(\,\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})-1,\ 0,\ 1\,\big), (8.1)

where α:=1/2\alpha:=1/2 is set by DAPO’s reward scale and is not tuned (derived in Section 9). Its reward R~DAPO:=R−PDAPO\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{DAPO}}:=R-P_{\mathrm{DAPO}} extends DAPO from one cap fixed before training to a budget sampled each episode. Its fixed coefficient penalises how far a policy overspends but not how often. Exp-Mag instead decays a success exponentially in the overspend, R​e−2​(C¯−1)+R\,e^{-2(\bar{C}-1)_{+}}, and leaves every failure at 00.

A per-budget constrained objective.

A cost penalty sets a single trade-off between success and spending, but does not directly control how often the policy overspends. To define the Rate and Dual objectives, we instead maximise success subject to a separate constraint on the probability of overspending at each budget. This gives the constrained objective

maxπ∈Π𝔼x∼p𝒳,B0∼pBζ∼π(⋅∣x,B0)​[R⁡(ζ)]s.t. ℙx∼p𝒳ζ∼π(⋅∣x,b)​(C¯​(ζ,b)>1)≤δ,∀b∈ℬ,\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \ \mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}},\ B_{0}\sim p_{B}\\ \zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,B_{0})\end{subarray}}\!\big[\,R(\zeta)\,\big]\quad\text{s.t. }\ \ \mathbb{P}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}}\\ \zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,b)\end{subarray}}\!\big(\,\bar{C}(\zeta,b)>1\,\big)\leq\delta,\quad\forall\,b\in\mathcal{B}, (8.2)

where δ∈(0,1)\delta\in(0,1) is the permitted overspend rate. The objective averages over tasks and budgets together, whereas each constraint conditions on the budget and averages over tasks alone, so it is the overspend rate a user would measure at budget bb across the distribution of tasks that they wish to have completed. Slack may therefore move between tasks but never between budgets.

Subtracting PDAPOP_{\mathrm{DAPO}} from the objective of Equation 8.2, with the constraints unchanged, gives our Dual training objective,

maxπ∈Π⁡𝔼x∼p𝒳,B0∼pBζ∼π(⋅∣x,B0)​[R⁡(ζ)−PDAPO​(ζ,B0)]​s.t. ​ℙx∼p𝒳ζ∼π(⋅∣x,b)​(C¯​(ζ,b)>1)≤δ,∀b∈ℬ.\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\ \ \mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}},\ B_{0}\sim p_{B}\\ \zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,B_{0})\end{subarray}}\!\big[\,R(\zeta)-P_{\mathrm{DAPO}}(\zeta,B_{0})\,\big]\hskip 9.24994pt\text{s.t. }\ \ \mathbb{P}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}}\\ \zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,b)\end{subarray}}\!\big(\,\bar{C}(\zeta,b)>1\,\big)\leq\delta,\hskip 9.24994pt\forall\,b\in\mathcal{B}. (8.3)

Lagrangian relaxation.

Introducing a non-negative multiplier λb\lambda_{b} for each budget-specific constraint gives the Lagrangian for Rate:

ℒrate(π,{λb})=𝔼x∼p𝒳,B0∼pBζ∼π(⋅∣x,B0)[R(ζ)−ΛB0 1[C¯(ζ,B0)>1]]+δ∑b∈ℬλb.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{rate}}\big(\pi,\{\lambda_{b}\}\big)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}},\ B_{0}\sim p_{B}\\ \zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,B_{0})\end{subarray}}\!\big[\,R(\zeta)-\Lambda_{B_{0}}\,\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1]\,\big]+\delta\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\lambda_{b}. (8.4)

Adding the DAPO magnitude penalty gives the Lagrangian for Dual:

ℒdual(π,{λb})=𝔼x∼p𝒳,B0∼pBζ∼π(⋅∣x,B0)[R(ζ)−PDAPO(ζ,B0)−ΛB0 1[C¯(ζ,B0)>1]]+δ∑b∈ℬλb.\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dual}}\big(\pi,\{\lambda_{b}\}\big)=\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}},\ B_{0}\sim p_{B}\\ \zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,B_{0})\end{subarray}}\!\big[\,R(\zeta)-P_{\mathrm{DAPO}}(\zeta,B_{0})-\Lambda_{B_{0}}\,\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1]\,\big]+\delta\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\lambda_{b}. (8.5)

Here Λb:=λb/pB​(b)\Lambda_{b}:=\lambda_{b}/p_{B}(b) is the effective price of overspending at budget bb; the factor 1/pB​(b)1/p_{B}(b) corrects for how often that budget is sampled. The final term is constant in π\pi, leaving the per-trajectory shaped return used by each method. In particular, R~rate:=R−ΛB0𝟏[C¯>1]\tilde{R}_{\mathrm{rate}}:=R-\Lambda_{B_{0}}\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}>1], and Dual additionally subtracts PDAPOP_{\mathrm{DAPO}}. Both methods update the multipliers in response to the overspend rate at each budget (Section 10.7). The rate penalty targets how often the policy overspends, while PDAPOP_{\mathrm{DAPO}} in Dual additionally distinguishes overspending trajectories by how far they exceed the budget (Section 10.5).

9 Adapting DAPO to Multi-Budget Settings

We give DAPO’s original soft-overlong penalty and show how we adapt it from a single fixed token cap to a family of budgets.

DAPO (Yu et al., 2026) introduces a soft-overlong penalty for truncated responses in long-chain-of-thought reinforcement learning, evaluated on mathematical reasoning tasks. The penalty increases with response length within a soft window near the maximum generation length. Given a maximum response length Lmax∈ℤ>0L_{\max}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} and a soft window Ls∈ℤ>0L_{\mathrm{s}}\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} with Ls≤LmaxL_{\mathrm{s}}\leq L_{\max}, it shapes the reward according to the response length L⁡(o)∈ℤ≥0L(o)\in\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0} as

Rlen​(o)={0,L⁡(o)≤Lmax−Ls,(Lmax−Ls)−L⁡(o)Ls,Lmax−Ls<L⁡(o)≤Lmax,−1,L⁡(o)>Lmax.R_{\mathrm{len}}(o)=\begin{cases}0,&L(o)\leq L_{\max}-L_{\mathrm{s}},\\[4.0pt] \dfrac{(L_{\max}-L_{\mathrm{s}})-L(o)}{L_{\mathrm{s}}},&L_{\max}-L_{\mathrm{s}}<L(o)\leq L_{\max},\\[4.0pt] -1,&L(o)>L_{\max}.\end{cases} (9.1)

The penalty is zero up to the soft threshold Lmax−LsL_{\max}-L_{\mathrm{s}}, decreases linearly to −1-1 over a window of width LsL_{\mathrm{s}}, and remains at −1-1 beyond LmaxL_{\max}. It therefore supplies a continuous penalty based on overspend magnitude.

This construction was designed for a single token-length cap fixed before training. Our setting instead requires one policy to work across a family of budgets B0B_{0}, with the budget varying between episodes, and with budgeted quantities other than tokens, such as steps or tool calls. We adapt DAPO’s penalty to this setting by expressing spend relative to the budget of the current episode.

Concretely, set Ls=B0L_{\mathrm{s}}=B_{0} and Lmax=2​B0L_{\max}=2B_{0} in Equation 9.1. The soft threshold Lmax−LsL_{\max}-L_{\mathrm{s}} is then exactly B0B_{0}, and the middle branch becomes

(2​B0−B0)−L⁡(o)B0=B0−L⁡(o)B0=−(L⁡(o)B0−1).\frac{(2B_{0}-B_{0})-L(o)}{B_{0}}=\frac{B_{0}-L(o)}{B_{0}}=-\left(\frac{L(o)}{B_{0}}-1\right). (9.2)

We therefore apply the linear ramp to the normalised trajectory cost C¯​(ζ,B0)\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0}) of Equation 3.6 instead of to the raw token count L⁡(o)L(o) against one fixed cap. Reversing the sign so that it is written as a positive penalty to be subtracted from the return gives the same ramp in normalised-cost units, clip⁡(C¯​(ζ,B0)−1, 0, 1).\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})-1,\,0,\,1\right). The cost map κ\kappa determines the quantity being budgeted, while normalisation by B0B_{0} makes the soft threshold C¯​(ζ,B0)=1\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})=1 for every budget. The same DAPO penalty therefore applies to any budget and to any cost unit.

It remains to match the scale of DAPO’s original reward. DAPO pairs a task reward RDAPO∈{−1,+1}R_{\mathrm{DAPO}}\in\{-1,+1\} with a penalty Rlen∈[−1,0]R_{\mathrm{len}}\in[-1,0], whereas our terminal reward R⁡(ζ)∈{0,1}R(\zeta)\in\{0,1\}. The map x↦(x+1)/2x\mapsto(x+1)/2 takes DAPO’s task-reward scale to ours. Applying the same map to DAPO’s shaped return gives

RDAPO+Rlen+12=RDAPO+12⏟R⁡(ζ)+12​Rlen,\frac{R_{\mathrm{DAPO}}+R_{\mathrm{len}}+1}{2}=\underbrace{\frac{R_{\mathrm{DAPO}}+1}{2}}_{R(\zeta)}\;+\;\tfrac{1}{2}R_{\mathrm{len}}, (9.3)

so preserving DAPO’s relative weighting between task success and the soft-overlong penalty introduces a factor of 12\tfrac{1}{2}. Combining this rescaling with the normalised expression above gives our penalty

PDAPO​(ζ,B0)=12​clip⁡(C¯​(ζ,B0)−1, 0, 1),P_{\mathrm{DAPO}}(\zeta,B_{0})=\tfrac{1}{2}\operatorname{clip}\!\left(\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})-1,\,0,\,1\right), (9.4)

which is Equation 8.1 with α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2}. We therefore set α=0.5\alpha=0.5 throughout (Section 11.7). In raw spend, CC, the penalty has slope 1/(2​B0)1/(2B_{0}) within the linear overspending region, so a fixed absolute overspend carries a larger penalty under a tighter budget than under a looser budget.

The rescaling preserves the relative weighting of task success and the length penalty. The Dr. GRPO advantage centres each trajectory’s return within its group (Section 10.7), so an affine transformation R~↦a​R~+c\tilde{R}\mapsto a\tilde{R}+c with a>0a>0 removes the additive constant under centring and multiplies every advantage by aa. For the unfiltered surrogate, this preserves the advantage signs and relative magnitudes and rescales its gradient by a constant.

10 Optimising Budget-Conditioned Objectives

This appendix describes the optimisation used in Section 3. Section 10.2 fixes the policy class and constraint functionals, Section 10.3 verifies the rearrangement of the Lagrangian Equation 8.5, Section 10.4 derives the policy and multiplier updates of Section 10.7 from it, and Section 10.5 explains the distinct signals supplied by Dual’s two penalties. Sections 10.6 and 10.7 give the shared Dr. GRPO policy update and the additional multiplier updates used by Rate and Dual. Section 10.8 gives a general training algorithm for fixed reward objectives, followed by the shared algorithm for Rate and Dual.

10.1 Background

Constrained MDPs (cMDPs) typically bound expected cumulative cost for a single fixed threshold (Altman, 2021; Achiam et al., 2017), often using Lagrangian methods for optimisation (Stooke et al., 2020). Budgeted MDPs (Carrara et al., 2019) extend cMDPs to families of budgets by conditioning value functions on the remaining allowance, but still constrain expected discounted cost return via fitted Q-iteration. This does not directly express budget compliance at the level of individual requests, where an expected-cost constraint can hide frequent individual violations. Risk-aware and chance-constrained formulations instead bound the probability of undesirable events (Geibel and Wysotzki, 2005; Haskell and Jain, 2015), and Chow (2017) studies trajectory-level probabilistic constraints under Lagrangian relaxation.

10.2 Setup

Throughout we work with the trajectory law induced by a policy π\pi on the budget-augmented POMDP ℳ~\tilde{\mathcal{M}} of Section 3.2. We write ℙπ\mathbb{P}_{\pi} for that law, i.e. ℙπ(⋅)=ℙx∼p𝒳,B0∼pB,ζ∼π(⋅∣x,B0)(⋅)\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(\cdot)=\mathbb{P}_{x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}},\ B_{0}\sim p_{B},\ \zeta\sim\pi(\cdot\mid x,B_{0})}(\cdot) and likewise 𝔼π\mathbb{E}_{\pi} for expectation under it, matching the sampling made explicit in Equations 8.2 and 8.5. We include the task draw in this law rather than writing it separately because every quantity below averages over tasks. Conditioning on a fixed budget, written ℙπ(⋅∣B0=b)\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(\cdot\mid B_{0}=b) below, still draws x∼p𝒳x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}} and then rolls out ζ\zeta under π(⋅∣x,b)\pi(\cdot\mid x,b). We define the objective and per-budget constraint functionals

J⁡(π):=𝔼π​[R⁡(ζ)],gb​(π):=ℙπ​(C¯​(ζ,B0)>1|B0=b)−δ,b∈ℬ,J(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\,R(\zeta)\,\right],\qquad g_{b}(\pi):=\mathbb{P}_{\pi}\!\left(\,\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1\,\middle|\,B_{0}=b\,\right)-\delta,\qquad b\in\mathcal{B}, (10.1)

so that the constrained objective Equation 8.2 reads maxπ∈Π⁡J⁡(π)\max_{\pi\in\Pi}J(\pi) subject to gb​(π)≤0g_{b}(\pi)\leq 0 for every b∈ℬb\in\mathcal{B}. The conditioning in Equation 10.1 is well-defined because pBp_{B} has full support on the finite set ℬ\mathcal{B}. Equation 8.3 keeps these constraints and shapes the objective,

J~​(π):=𝔼π​[R⁡(ζ)−PDAPO​(ζ,B0)],\tilde{J}(\pi):=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\,R(\zeta)-P_{\mathrm{DAPO}}(\zeta,B_{0})\,\right], (10.2)

so that it reads maxπ∈Π⁡J~​(π)\max_{\pi\in\Pi}\tilde{J}(\pi) subject to the same gb​(π)≤0g_{b}(\pi)\leq 0. Its Lagrangian is ℒdual\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{dual}} in Equation 8.5, which we abbreviate as ℒ\mathcal{L} below. Results below are stated for J~\tilde{J}, and setting α=0\alpha=0 recovers JJ and Equation 8.2.

10.3 Rearrangement of the Lagrangian

Relaxing Equation 8.3 prices each budget with its own multiplier, through the penalty

∑b∈ℬλb​(ℙπ​(C¯​(ζ,B0)>1∣B0=b)−δ).\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\lambda_{b}\big(\mathbb{P}_{\pi}(\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1\mid B_{0}=b)-\delta\big).

Folding that sum into a single expectation produces the compact Lagrangian Equation 8.5 and its per-trajectory integrand, the shaped return of Dual (Figure 1). Writing each overspend probability as an expectation and splitting the outer expectation over the prior B0∼pBB_{0}\sim p_{B},

∑b∈ℬλb​ℙπ​(C¯​(ζ,B0)>1|B0=b)\displaystyle\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\lambda_{b}\,\mathbb{P}_{\pi}\!\left(\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1\,\middle|\,B_{0}=b\right) =∑b∈ℬλb𝔼π[ 1[C¯(ζ,B0)>1]|B0=b]\displaystyle=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\lambda_{b}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\,\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1]\,\middle|\,B_{0}=b\,\right]
=∑b∈ℬpB(b)λbpB​(b)𝔼π[ 1[C¯(ζ,B0)>1]|B0=b]\displaystyle=\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}p_{B}(b)\,\frac{\lambda_{b}}{p_{B}(b)}\,\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\,\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1]\,\middle|\,B_{0}=b\,\right]
=𝔼π[λB0pB​(B0) 1[C¯(ζ,B0)>1]],\displaystyle=\mathbb{E}_{\pi}\!\left[\,\frac{\lambda_{B_{0}}}{p_{B}(B_{0})}\,\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1]\,\right], (10.3)

where the second line divides and multiplies by pB​(b)>0p_{B}(b)>0 and the third recognises the resulting sum as an expectation over B0∼pBB_{0}\sim p_{B}. The importance weight 1/pB​(B0)1/p_{B}(B_{0}) therefore corrects for the frequency with which each budget is sampled, so that a budget contributes to the penalty in proportion to λb\lambda_{b} alone and not to how often it is drawn. The remaining term δ​∑bλb\delta\sum_{b}\lambda_{b} is constant in π\pi and plays no part in the policy update. Under the uniform prior used in our experiments, 1/pB​(b)=|ℬ|1/p_{B}(b)=|\mathcal{B}| for every budget, so the effective price appearing in the shaped return is Λb=|ℬ|​λb\Lambda_{b}=|\mathcal{B}|\,\lambda_{b}.

10.4 Gradients of the Lagrangian

This section derives the policy and multiplier updates of Section 10.7 from the Lagrangian Equation 8.5, whose per-trajectory integrand is the shaped return R~\tilde{R} of Dual (Figure 1) and whose trailing term δ​∑b∈ℬλb\delta\sum_{b\in\mathcal{B}}\lambda_{b} is constant in π\pi.

Policy gradient.

Fix {λb}\{\lambda_{b}\} and parameterise the policy by πθ\pi_{\theta} as in Equation 3.4. In the budget-augmented POMDP ℳ~\tilde{\mathcal{M}} of Section 3.2, neither the kernels 𝒯~,𝒪~\tilde{\mathcal{T}},\tilde{\mathcal{O}} nor the budget recursion bt+1=bt−κ⁡(at)b_{t+1}=b_{t}-\kappa(a_{t}) depends on θ\theta, so their log-derivatives vanish and the trajectory score reduces to a sum over the policy’s own factors,

sθ​(ζ,x,B0):=∇θ​log​pθ​(ζ∣x,B0)=∑t≤τ∇θ​log​πθ​(at∣x,ht,bt,B0).s_{\theta}(\zeta,x,B_{0}):=\nabla_{\theta}\log p_{\theta}(\zeta\mid x,B_{0})=\sum_{t\leq\tau}\nabla_{\theta}\log\pi_{\theta}\!\left(a_{t}\mid x,h_{t},b_{t},B_{0}\right). (10.4)

Since δ​∑bλb\delta\sum_{b}\lambda_{b} is constant in π\pi, the score-function gradient of the Lagrangian is

∇θℒ(πθ,{λb})=𝔼x∼p𝒳,B0∼pB,ζ∼πθ(⋅∣x,B0)[R~(ζ,B0)sθ(ζ,x,B0)].\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}\big(\pi_{\theta},\{\lambda_{b}\}\big)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\mathcal{X}},\,B_{0}\sim p_{B},\,\zeta\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,B_{0})}\!\left[\,\tilde{R}(\zeta,B_{0})\,s_{\theta}(\zeta,x,B_{0})\right]. (10.5)

Each action ata_{t} is itself a token sequence, so each factor of Equation 10.4 expands into per-token log-probabilities and sθs_{\theta} sums over all generated tokens. The return is terminal and undiscounted, so Equation 10.5 weights every token of a trajectory by the same scalar R~\tilde{R}, with no length normaliser.

We reduce variance by centring returns within each group. Write

R~(g,i):=R~​(ζ(g,i),B0(g)),sθ(g,i):=sθ​(ζ(g,i),x(g),B0(g)),R~¯(g):=G−1​∑j=1GR~(g,j).\tilde{R}^{(g,i)}:=\tilde{R}\big(\zeta^{(g,i)},B_{0}^{(g)}\big),\qquad s_{\theta}^{(g,i)}:=s_{\theta}\big(\zeta^{(g,i)},x^{(g)},B_{0}^{(g)}\big),\qquad\bar{\tilde{R}}^{(g)}:=G^{-1}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\tilde{R}^{(g,j)}.

Within a group, trajectories are i.i.d. given the task and budget. Given that pair, 𝔼ζ∼πθ(⋅∣x,B0)[sθ(ζ,x,B0)]=0\mathbb{E}_{\zeta\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x,B_{0})}[s_{\theta}(\zeta,x,B_{0})]=0, so the cross terms vanish. Each trajectory also appears in its own group mean, leaving a factor of 1−1/G1-1/G after averaging over the task and budget draws,

𝔼(x(g),B0(g))∼p𝒳⊗pBζ(g,1),…,ζ(g,G)∼πθ(⋅∣x(g),B0(g))​[(R~(g,i)−R~¯(g))​sθ(g,i)]=(1−1G)​∇θℒ​(πθ,{λb}),\mathbb{E}_{\begin{subarray}{c}(x^{(g)},B_{0}^{(g)})\,\sim\,p_{\mathcal{X}}\otimes p_{B}\\ \zeta^{(g,1)},\ldots,\zeta^{(g,G)}\,\sim\,\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x^{(g)},B_{0}^{(g)})\end{subarray}}\!\left[\left(\tilde{R}^{(g,i)}-\bar{\tilde{R}}^{(g)}\right)s_{\theta}^{(g,i)}\right]=\left(1-\frac{1}{G}\right)\nabla_{\theta}\mathcal{L}\big(\pi_{\theta},\{\lambda_{b}\}\big), (10.6)

with the constant absorbed into the learning rate. We omit GRPO’s standard-deviation and length normalisers of Equation 10.10, which do not preserve this gradient (Section 10.6).

In practice we replace Equation 10.5 by the clipped Dr. GRPO surrogate Equation 10.14, recovering the advantage Equation 10.13. Before the segment filtering of Section 11.6, its expected gradient agrees with the policy gradient up to the factor 1−1/G1-1/G at θ=θold\theta=\theta_{\mathrm{old}}, where every ratio rt,l(g,i)​(θ)r_{t,l}^{(g,i)}(\theta) equals one, while clipping controls the off-policy change over repeated optimisation steps on one batch of rollouts (Section 10.6).

Multiplier gradient.

Now fix π\pi and let pb:=ℙπ​(C¯​(ζ,B0)>1|B0=b)=gb​(π)+δp_{b}:=\mathbb{P}_{\pi}\!\left(\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1\,\middle|\,B_{0}=b\right)=g_{b}(\pi)+\delta be the overspend rate at budget bb. Differentiating Equation 8.5 in λb\lambda_{b}, with the penalty written per budget as in Equation 10.3, gives

∂ℒ∂λb=−gb​(π)=−(pb−δ).\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\lambda_{b}}=-g_{b}(\pi)=-(p_{b}-\delta). (10.7)

Since the multipliers minimise ℒ\mathcal{L} subject to λb≥0\lambda_{b}\geq 0, projected gradient descent in λb\lambda_{b} gives the projected dual update of Algorithm 2,

λb←[λb−β​∂ℒ∂λb]+=[λb+β⁡(pb−δ)]+.\lambda_{b}\leftarrow\left[\,\lambda_{b}-\beta\frac{\partial\mathcal{L}}{\partial\lambda_{b}}\,\right]_{+}=\big[\,\lambda_{b}+\beta(p_{b}-\delta)\,\big]_{+}. (10.8)

Replacing pbp_{b} by the batch estimate p^b\hat{p}_{b} gives Equation 10.15. Each multiplier therefore increases when pb>δp_{b}>\delta and decreases when pb<δp_{b}<\delta, subject to projection at zero. The batch estimate p^b\hat{p}_{b} is unbiased for pbp_{b} under the current policy. We use it without smoothing across updates to keep the estimate on-policy. By Equation 10.7 the gradient at budget bb does not involve λb′\lambda_{b^{\prime}} for b′≠bb^{\prime}\neq b, so all multipliers update in parallel from one batch, as in Algorithm 2.

At a fixed point of the exact-rate update away from the upper cap in Equation 10.15, λb>0\lambda_{b}>0 implies pb=δp_{b}=\delta, while λb=0\lambda_{b}=0 implies pb≤δp_{b}\leq\delta. Thus, a budget with a positive, uncapped multiplier has overspend rate δ\delta.

10.5 Complementary Roles of the Two Penalties

Both penalties in the Dual return Equation 8.5 activate on the same event {C¯(ζ,B0)>1}\{\bar{C}(\zeta,B_{0})>1\} but act on different quantities. As a function of the normalised cost c=C¯​(ζ,b)c=\bar{C}(\zeta,b) at a fixed task outcome, the rate term Λb𝟏[c>1]\Lambda_{b}\mathbf{1}[c>1] is constant on {c>1}\{c>1\}, whereas PDAPOP_{\mathrm{DAPO}} of Equation 8.1 has slope α\alpha on (1,2)(1,2). The rate term alone is therefore indifferent between a marginal and a gross overspend. Conversely, α=12\alpha=\tfrac{1}{2} is fixed and shared across budgets, so the overspend rate it induces at any budget is not controlled, whereas an interior fixed point of the dual update gives pb=δp_{b}=\delta (Section 10.4).

What reaches the policy is the group-centred advantage Equation 10.13. Fix a group gg at budget bb and drop the index gg, writing R(i)R^{(i)} for the task reward of rollout ii, u(i):=𝟏[C¯(ζ(i),b)>1]u^{(i)}:=\mathbf{1}[\bar{C}(\zeta^{(i)},b)>1] for its overspend indicator, P(i):=PDAPO​(ζ(i),b)P^{(i)}:=P_{\mathrm{DAPO}}(\zeta^{(i)},b) for its magnitude penalty and p^:=G−1​∑ju(j)\hat{p}:=G^{-1}\sum_{j}u^{(j)} for the overspend fraction of the group. Centring each term of the return separately gives

A(i)=(R(i)−R¯)⏟task outcome−(P(i)−P¯)⏟magnitude−Λb​(u(i)−p^)⏟rate,A^{(i)}=\underbrace{\big(R^{(i)}-\bar{R}\big)}_{\text{task outcome}}\;-\;\underbrace{\big(P^{(i)}-\bar{P}\big)}_{\text{magnitude}}\;-\;\underbrace{\Lambda_{b}\big(u^{(i)}-\hat{p}\big)}_{\text{rate}}, (10.9)

with bars denoting group means. Which terms survive depends on how the group splits on the budget. If no rollout overspends, both penalty terms vanish and the group reduces to ordinary task learning whatever Λb\Lambda_{b} has reached. If every rollout overspends, the rate term cancels however large Λb\Lambda_{b} is, and only differences in the magnitude penalty distinguish rollouts with the same task outcome. This signal also vanishes if every magnitude penalty has saturated. Without it, a group that also shares its task outcome has zero advantage. Such groups can occur at tight budgets early in training, when every rollout overspends and none succeeds; rate-only shaping then supplies no policy-gradient signal. If compliance is mixed, the rate term separates compliant from overspending rollouts by exactly Λb\Lambda_{b} however far the overspenders ran over, while the magnitude term orders the overspending rollouts by at most α\alpha. The dual therefore sets the price of overspending at all, adjusted per budget towards the target rate δ\delta, and PDAPOP_{\mathrm{DAPO}} orders overspending trajectories by how far they ran over. Neither is recoverable from the other by rescaling, so Dual keeps both.

10.6 Group-Relative Policy Optimisation

GRPO (Shao et al., 2024) is a critic-free variant of PPO (Schulman et al., 2017). For each prompt, it samples a group of G∈ℤ>0G\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} responses with rewards {r(g,i)}i=1G⊂ℝ\{r^{(g,i)}\}_{i=1}^{G}\subset\mathbb{R} and uses the group mean as a baseline. For each group gg, its advantage is

A(g,i)=1σ(g)​(r(g,i)−1G​∑j=1Gr(g,j)),A^{(g,i)}=\frac{1}{\sigma^{(g)}}\left(r^{(g,i)}-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}r^{(g,j)}\right), (10.10)

where σ(g)\sigma^{(g)} is the standard deviation of the rewards within group gg. This expression applies to groups with nonzero reward variance. GRPO applies this advantage to each response token through a clipped PPO surrogate, averaging the token-level objective within each response. For a batch of KK groups with GG responses per group, this objective is

𝒥GRPO​(θ)=1K​G​∑g=1K∑i=1G1N(g,i)​∑t≤τ(g,i)∑l≤Lt(g,i)min⁡(rt,l(g,i)​(θ)​A(g,i),clip⁡(rt,l(g,i)​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​A(g,i)),\mathcal{J}_{\mathrm{GRPO}}(\theta)=\frac{1}{KG}\sum_{g=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\frac{1}{N^{(g,i)}}\sum_{t\leq\tau^{(g,i)}}\sum_{l\leq L_{t}^{(g,i)}}\min\!\left(r_{t,l}^{(g,i)}(\theta)A^{(g,i)},\operatorname{clip}\!\left(r_{t,l}^{(g,i)}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)A^{(g,i)}\right), (10.11)

where N(g,i):=∑t≤τ(g,i)Lt(g,i)N^{(g,i)}:=\sum_{t\leq\tau^{(g,i)}}L_{t}^{(g,i)} is the total number of generated tokens in trajectory (g,i)(g,i), and rt,l(g,i)​(θ)r_{t,l}^{(g,i)}(\theta) is the token-level importance ratio between the current and behaviour policies.

Liu et al. (2025c) identify biases from both normalisers in these equations. Dividing by σ\sigma gives greater weight to groups with lower reward variance. Dividing the surrogate by response length gives shorter positive-advantage responses larger per-token updates, while giving longer negative-advantage responses smaller per-token updates. This can encourage failed responses to grow longer. Dr. GRPO removes both normalisers, using

A(g,i)=r(g,i)−1G​∑j=1Gr(g,j)A^{(g,i)}=r^{(g,i)}-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}r^{(g,j)} (10.12)

and summing the clipped surrogate over response tokens without dividing by response length. The batch averaging factor 1/(K​G)1/(KG) remains.

We use Dr. GRPO throughout, grouping trajectories by task and budget so that the within-group baseline compares rollouts subject to the same budget. Section 10.7 gives the resulting policy update for our shaped return.

10.7 Policy and Multiplier Updates

Policy update.

At each iteration, we draw K∈ℤ>0K\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} task-budget pairs (x(g),B0(g))∼p𝒳⊗pB(x^{(g)},B_{0}^{(g)})\sim p_{\mathcal{X}}\otimes p_{B}, g=1,…,Kg=1,\ldots,K, and sample G∈ℤ>0G\in\mathbb{Z}_{>0} trajectories ζ(g,i)∼πθ(⋅∣x(g),B0(g))\zeta^{(g,i)}\sim\pi_{\theta}(\cdot\mid x^{(g)},B_{0}^{(g)}), i=1,…,Gi=1,\ldots,G, for each pair. Writing R~(g,i):=R~​(ζ(g,i),B0(g))∈ℝ\tilde{R}^{(g,i)}:=\tilde{R}(\zeta^{(g,i)},B_{0}^{(g)})\in\mathbb{R} for the chosen training return, we centre it within each group:

A(g,i)=R~(g,i)−1G​∑j=1GR~(g,j).A^{(g,i)}=\tilde{R}^{(g,i)}-\frac{1}{G}\sum_{j=1}^{G}\tilde{R}^{(g,j)}. (10.13)

Each group therefore contains rollouts for one task at one budget. For Rate and Dual, the group also shares the same multiplier λB0(g)\lambda_{B_{0}^{(g)}}. Centring within groups compares trajectories that faced identical budgets. This is Equation 10.12 with r(i)r^{(i)} replaced by R~(g,i)\tilde{R}^{(g,i)}.

At step tt, collect the policy’s inputs into zt(g,i):=(x(g),ht(g,i),bt(g,i),B0(g))z_{t}^{(g,i)}:=\big(x^{(g)},h_{t}^{(g,i)},b_{t}^{(g,i)},B_{0}^{(g)}\big) and write the action as its token sequence at(g,i)=(at,1(g,i),…,at,Lt(g,i)(g,i))a_{t}^{(g,i)}=\big(a_{t,1}^{(g,i)},\dots,a_{t,L_{t}^{(g,i)}}^{(g,i)}\big). The token-level importance ratio is

rt,l(g,i)​(θ)=πθ​(at,l(g,i)∣zt(g,i),at,<l(g,i))πθold​(at,l(g,i)∣zt(g,i),at,<l(g,i)).r_{t,l}^{(g,i)}(\theta)=\frac{\pi_{\theta}\!\big(a_{t,l}^{(g,i)}\mid z_{t}^{(g,i)},a_{t,<l}^{(g,i)}\big)}{\pi_{\theta_{\mathrm{old}}}\!\big(a_{t,l}^{(g,i)}\mid z_{t}^{(g,i)},a_{t,<l}^{(g,i)}\big)}.

For clip range ϵ∈(0,1)\epsilon\in(0,1), we ascend the Dr. GRPO surrogate

𝒥⁡(θ)=1K​G​∑g=1K∑i=1G∑t≤τ(g,i)∑l≤Lt(g,i)min⁡(rt,l(g,i)​(θ)​A(g,i),clip⁡(rt,l(g,i)​(θ),1−ϵ,1+ϵ)​A(g,i)).\mathcal{J}(\theta)=\frac{1}{KG}\sum_{g=1}^{K}\sum_{i=1}^{G}\sum_{t\leq\tau^{(g,i)}}\sum_{l\leq L_{t}^{(g,i)}}\min\!\left(r_{t,l}^{(g,i)}(\theta)A^{(g,i)},\operatorname{clip}\!\left(r_{t,l}^{(g,i)}(\theta),1-\epsilon,1+\epsilon\right)A^{(g,i)}\right). (10.14)

As in Dr. GRPO, the trajectory-level advantage is applied to every token without a response-length normaliser. This policy update applies to every reward objective. For Dual, Section 10.4 relates it to the policy gradient of Equation 8.5.

Multiplier update.

For Rate and Dual, each multiplier λb\lambda_{b} increases when the policy overspends at budget bb more often than the permitted rate δ\delta, and decreases otherwise. We estimate the overspend rate from the batch rollouts collected at budget bb, pooled over their tasks. Let

C¯(g,i):=C¯​(ζ(g,i),B0(g)),ℐb:={(g,i):B0(g)=b},\bar{C}^{(g,i)}:=\bar{C}\big(\zeta^{(g,i)},B_{0}^{(g)}\big),\qquad\mathcal{I}_{b}:=\{(g,i):B_{0}^{(g)}=b\},

and let β∈ℝ>0\beta\in\mathbb{R}_{>0} be the multiplier step size. The batch estimate and projected update are

p^b=1|ℐb|∑(g,i)∈ℐb[C¯(g,i)>1],λb←min{[λb+β(p^b−δ)]+,ΛmaxpB(b)}.\hat{p}_{b}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{I}_{b}|}\sum_{(g,i)\in\mathcal{I}_{b}}\mathbf{1}\!\left[\bar{C}^{(g,i)}>1\right],\qquad\lambda_{b}\leftarrow\min\!\left\{\big[\lambda_{b}+\beta(\hat{p}_{b}-\delta)\big]_{+},\,\Lambda_{\max}p_{B}(b)\right\}. (10.15)

For budgets with |ℐb|>0|\mathcal{I}_{b}|>0, this is projected gradient descent on the Lagrangian in λb\lambda_{b}, whose gradient at the true overspend rate pbp_{b} is δ−pb\delta-p_{b} (Section 10.4). Budgets absent from the batch retain their previous multiplier. The raw batch estimate is not smoothed across updates, keeping the multiplier update on-policy.

The effective-price cap Λmax\Lambda_{\max} depends on the reward. For Rate, which has no magnitude penalty, we set Λmax=1\Lambda_{\max}=1. For Dual, we set Λmax=12\Lambda_{\max}=\tfrac{1}{2} because the DAPO penalty is also bounded by 12\tfrac{1}{2}. In each case, the cap ensures that an overspending success is not valued below a compliant failure. We project the multiplier itself, rather than clipping only the price in the shaped return, so that the price can decrease when the overspend rate falls below δ\delta. The cap makes this a bounded-price relaxation: a budget can retain an overspend rate above δ\delta when its price reaches the cap, and we do not claim constraint satisfaction or convergence for the parameterised policy.

10.8 Training Algorithms

Algorithm 1 optimises Equation 3.5 for a chosen fixed return R~\tilde{R}. For simplicity, both algorithms sample budgets uniformly from ℬ\mathcal{B}, as in our experiments. Rollouts receive budget feedback and end on agent or environment termination, or at TmaxT_{\max}. GRPO-Std sets R~​(ζ,B0)=R⁡(ζ)\tilde{R}(\zeta,B_{0})=R(\zeta), while the fixed budget-shaped objectives use the returns in Section 8. Trunc also applies its budget cutoff. Both algorithms use the segment filtering described in Section 11.6.

Algorithm 2 covers Rate and Dual by adding a learned violation price and updating it from the same rollouts. Under uniform budget sampling, the effective price is Λb=|ℬ|​λb\Lambda_{b}=|\mathcal{B}|\lambda_{b}.

11 Experimental Setup

We describe the environments, data splits, cost maps, budget grids, and budget-conditioning instructions used in our experiments. Each environment uses the budget-augmented POMDP of Section 3.2. The total budget B0B_{0} is given at the start of the episode, and the remaining budget btb_{t} is reported after each turn. All evaluations use four rollouts per evaluation instance and budget, while training uses groups of eight rollouts.

11.1 AppWorld

AppWorld (Trivedi et al., 2024) is an interactive coding-agent benchmark in which the agent completes digital tasks by writing Python code that calls simulated app APIs. Each executed code block is one model turn, including the terminal apis.supervisor.complete_task() call.

We train on the AppWorld training split and evaluate on the 168168 tasks in test-normal. With four rollouts per task, this gives 672672 rollouts per budget. We also evaluate under distribution shift on the 417417 tasks in test-challenge. AppWorld labels each task as easy, medium, or hard, which we use to split spend by difficulty in Figure 4(a). Unless stated otherwise, uncertainty bands for binary success and compliance rates show ±1\pm 1 standard deviation of the binomial rate estimate.

Episodes have a horizon of Tmax=40T_{\max}=40 turns for Qwen3.5-9B and Tmax=50T_{\max}=50 turns for Qwen3.5-4B. These horizons exceed the largest training step budgets, allowing overspending to remain observable rather than being hidden by the episode horizon.

11.2 ASTRA

ASTRA is a personal-assistant benchmark built on ToolSandbox (Lu et al., 2025), with tasks involving email, calendars, messages, and contacts. Its native interface uses structured tool calls, whereas AppWorld uses Python code. We expose all ASTRA tools through a single all namespace and retain AppWorld’s Python-REPL interface. Calls therefore take the form apis.all.api_name(kwarg=val). This keeps the action interface aligned with AppWorld for the transfer experiments of Section 4.3. ASTRA grades success by similarity to a set of reference milestones. We binarise this score at a threshold of 0.80.8 for our evaluation.

We use ASTRA only to evaluate the AppWorld-trained policies without retraining. The evaluation covers 31163116 ASTRA scenarios under step budgets from 22 to 1414, with a horizon of 4040 turns. It uses the AppWorld step-budget block of Section 11.5. The ASTRA task instruction retains the AppWorld REPL framing and general instructions where possible and differs only where required by the ASTRA tool interface. Sections 11.5 and 11.5 give both task instructions in full.

11.3 BabyAI

We use a text interface to BabyAI (Chevalier-Boisvert et al., 2019), a partially observed gridworld environment built on MiniGrid. The agent receives textual observations and selects moves from a small fixed vocabulary, including turn left, turn right, move forward, pick up, drop, and toggle. This provides a task and environment type distinct from the multi-turn coding settings of AppWorld and ASTRA.

We budget BabyAI by model turns rather than individual moves. Each action block may contain multiple moves and costs one unit regardless of how many moves it contains. This parallels the AppWorld step budget, where an agent can batch multiple API calls within a single turn. The moves execute sequentially without intermediate observations. An invalid move invalidates the entire block while still consuming the turn. The agent can therefore conserve budget by batching moves, at the cost of acting further ahead without observing intermediate states.

We use 1515 BabyAI levels covering a range of navigation and object-interaction tasks. Each level defines a family of related tasks rather than a single fixed environment. We generate concrete task instances from each level using fixed random seeds. A seed determines the mission, environment layout, object and door placement, and the agent’s initial state.

We construct non-overlapping training and evaluation sets using disjoint seed pools. No concrete task instance therefore appears in both splits, although both cover the same level families. The evaluation seeds are fixed and shared across methods, so every policy is evaluated on the same missions and environment configurations.

11.4 Cost Maps and Budgeted Quantities

We vary the budgeted quantity through the cost map κ\kappa while leaving the rest of the training framework unchanged. Table 4 gives the three cost maps used in our experiments.

Under a step budget, each model turn costs one unit. On BabyAI, one model turn may contain several primitive moves. Under a tool-call budget, each API call is charged independently. Under a token budget, all tokens generated by the policy are charged, including its reasoning and actions. Tokens in the task instruction and environment observations are not charged.

Budget grids.

On AppWorld, we construct a separate six point training grid for each model and cost unit. The grid is based on the empirical resource use of GRPO-Std, trained with the shared Dr. GRPO pipeline and a budget-independent task reward. We select budgets at the 11st, 1010th, 2525th, 5050th, 7575th, and 9090th percentiles of its spend distribution. This produces budgets spanning the observed range of task demands, from highly constrained settings to comparatively generous ones. All reward formulations use the same training and evaluation grids within each model and cost unit.

All AppWorld evaluation grids include training budgets and unseen budgets between the training points. The step and API-call grids also include budgets below and above the training range; the token grids remain within it. Table 5 gives the grids. For BabyAI, all methods and both model scales use the same six turn budgets, {5,7,11,16,23,34}\{5,7,11,16,23,34\}, for training and evaluation.

11.5 Budget Conditioning and Prompt Templates

At the start of each episode, the policy receives a domain-specific task instruction followed immediately by a <budget> block. The block states the total budget B0B_{0}. After every model turn, the environment appends the remaining budget btb_{t} to the next observation. The policy therefore observes both the original and remaining budgets throughout the episode, as required by Equation 3.4.

Section 11.5 gives the AppWorld task instruction, and Section 11.5 gives its ASTRA adaptation. AppWorld uses separate budget blocks for step, API-call, and token budgets, which are given in Sections 11.5, 11.5 and 11.5. Sections 11.5 and 11.5 give the BabyAI task instruction and turn-budget block. All models, methods, and splits within a domain and cost unit receive the same text. Only the task-specific fields and total budget vary, together with the user and date fields where applicable.

At every subsequent turn, the environment appends the remaining budget as <budget>Budget remaining btb_{t} of B0B_{0} {{ unit }}.</budget>, with the unit matching the cost map. Once the policy exceeds its budget, the message reports zero remaining and states how far the policy is over budget. Under a token budget, it also reports the tokens used by the preceding turn and repeats the request to estimate the length of the next turn.

The guidance differs by resource type because each budget can be conserved in a different way. Batching API calls into one code block conserves steps but does not conserve API calls. Token budgets charge both reasoning and code. BabyAI allows several primitive moves to be placed in one turn, but the agent receives no intermediate observation between those moves.

11.6 Models and Dr. GRPO Settings

We train Qwen3.5 at 4B and 9B parameters and report both scales throughout. Every method continues training from each model’s released post-trained checkpoint, with no supervised warm start of our own. All parameters are updated, with no LoRA, adapters, or frozen layers.

Optimisation uses the group-centred Dr. GRPO advantage Equation 10.13, with neither length nor standard-deviation normalisation, at γ=1\gamma=1, for 120120 updates on Qwen3.5-9B and 8080 on Qwen3.5-4B. The learning rate is flat at 3×10−63\times 10^{-6} with no schedule. Thinking is enabled, with a 768768-token allowance on Qwen3.5-9B and 512512 on Qwen3.5-4B. Under the step and tool-call cost maps these tokens do not count against the budget, whereas under the token cost map of Section 11.4 they are priced.

Each iteration draws KK groups (Equation 10.13), with K=8K=8 on Qwen3.5-9B and K=32K=32 on Qwen3.5-4B, each comprising G=8G=8 completions for a shared task and a shared budget, sampled at temperature 1.01.0 with nucleus and top-kk truncation disabled. The policy update is the clipped surrogate Equation 10.14 with symmetric clip range ϵ=0.2\epsilon=0.2 and no KL penalty or entropy bonus, so the return is shaped only by each method’s own objective (Section 3.3). Qwen3.5-9B takes 22 epochs per update with gradient accumulation over 88 microbatches of at most 44 segments, and Qwen3.5-4B takes 11 epoch over 22 microbatches of at most 88. Before the update, groups whose advantages are all zero are dropped, and negative-advantage segments are subsampled so that they make up at most a quarter of the batch. This additional sampling step changes the relative weighting of positive and negative advantages; the unfiltered gradient calculation in Section 10.4 does not establish unbiasedness of the implemented update.

11.7 Budget and Constraint Settings

Budgets are drawn uniformly from ℬ\mathcal{B}, so 1/pB​(b)=|ℬ|1/p_{B}(b)=|\mathcal{B}| and the effective price of Dual and Rate (Figure 1) is Λb=|ℬ|​λb\Lambda_{b}=|\mathcal{B}|\lambda_{b}. The AppWorld horizons of Section 11.1 exceed the largest training step budgets, so step-budget overspending remains observable to both the dual and soft-overlong penalties. The ramp of Equation 8.1 saturates at twice the budget, so under the step cost map it reaches its maximum of α\alpha only when 2​b≤Tmax2b\leq T_{\max}. On AppWorld, the top three budgets of the Qwen3.5-9B step grid and the top budget of the Qwen3.5-4B step grid fall outside this range. At these budgets, the penalty grades overspending across the entire reachable range without saturating.

We set the permitted overspend rate to δ=0.05\delta=0.05. The dual step size is β=0.01\beta=0.01 for Qwen3.5-9B and β=0.04\beta=0.04 for Qwen3.5-4B. Under the uniform six-rung budget prior, these give effective-price step sizes of |ℬ|​β=0.06|\mathcal{B}|\beta=0.06 and 0.240.24, respectively. We update the dual using the raw within-batch overspend rate in Equation 10.15, without smoothing across batches. The soft-overlong coefficient is α=0.5\alpha=0.5, following the reward-scale argument in Section 9.

Multipliers are initialised at λb=0\lambda_{b}=0 for every budget. For Rate, they are projected onto [0,pB​(b)]\big[0,p_{B}(b)\big], giving an effective-price cap of Λb≤1\Lambda_{b}\leq 1. For Dual, they are projected onto [0,(1−α)​pB​(b)]\big[0,(1-\alpha)p_{B}(b)\big], giving an effective-price cap of Λb≤1−α=0.5\Lambda_{b}\leq 1-\alpha=0.5. These are the largest prices for which an overspending success is not valued below a compliant failure under the corresponding reward formulation.

11.8 Compute

Training runs on 8×8\times B200 GPUs with tensor-parallel vLLM generation and an FSDP trainer. Evaluation runs on 8×8\times H100 GPUs for Qwen3.5-9B and 4×4\times H100 for Qwen3.5-4B.

What the dual costs to train.

Dual and Linear-Mag provide a direct comparison of the additional algorithmic cost of the dual update. The dual introduces only |ℬ||\mathcal{B}| scalar multipliers, which are updated once per iteration using Equation 10.15. It requires no additional model parameters, rollouts, forward passes, or backward passes. Both methods use the same rollout configuration, optimiser settings, and hardware. Their realised compute may nevertheless differ because the learned policies generate trajectories of different lengths and advantage filtering may retain different numbers of segments. We therefore treat the methods as matched in training configuration rather than claiming identical wall-clock or optimiser cost.

12 Additional Results

12.1 Across-Budget Utility Metrics

We define the summary metrics reported in Table 2. An evaluation setting is a combination of model scale, environment, and budget unit. We consider eight settings. These comprise AppWorld step, tool-call, and token budgets and BabyAI turn budgets for each of Qwen3.5-9B and Qwen3.5-4B.

We compare the ten budget-shaping mechanisms and exclude Base and GRPO-Std because their rewards do not depend on the budget.

Metrics.

Let ℛ\mathcal{R} denote the set of evaluation settings and let ℳr\mathcal{M}_{r} denote the methods evaluated in setting r∈ℛr\in\mathcal{R}. Let BrB_{r} be the evaluation budget grid for setting rr, and let 𝒰m,r​(b)\mathcal{U}_{m,r}(b) denote the observed budget utility of method mm at budget bb. The highest observed utility at each budget is

𝒰r∗​(b)=maxm∈ℳr⁡𝒰m,r​(b).\mathcal{U}^{*}_{r}(b)=\max_{m\in\mathcal{M}_{r}}\mathcal{U}_{m,r}(b). (12.1)

For each method mm, let ℛm⊆ℛ\mathcal{R}_{m}\subseteq\mathcal{R} contain the settings in which it was evaluated. We define

Win⁡(m)\displaystyle\mathrm{Win}(m) =1|ℛm|∑r∈ℛm1|Br|∑b∈Br𝟏[𝒰m,r(b)=𝒰r∗(b)],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}_{m}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{m}}\frac{1}{|B_{r}|}\sum_{b\in B_{r}}\mathbf{1}\left[\mathcal{U}_{m,r}(b)=\mathcal{U}^{*}_{r}(b)\right], (12.2)
NearBestϵ​(m)\displaystyle\mathrm{NearBest}_{\epsilon}(m) =1|ℛm|∑r∈ℛm1|Br|∑b∈Br𝟏[𝒰m,r(b)≥𝒰r∗(b)−ϵ],\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}_{m}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{m}}\frac{1}{|B_{r}|}\sum_{b\in B_{r}}\mathbf{1}\left[\mathcal{U}_{m,r}(b)\geq\mathcal{U}^{*}_{r}(b)-\epsilon\right], (12.3)
Regret⁡(m)\displaystyle\mathrm{Regret}(m) =1|ℛm|​∑r∈ℛm1|Br|​∑b∈Br[𝒰r∗​(b)−𝒰m,r​(b)].\displaystyle=\frac{1}{|\mathcal{R}_{m}|}\sum_{r\in\mathcal{R}_{m}}\frac{1}{|B_{r}|}\sum_{b\in B_{r}}\left[\mathcal{U}^{*}_{r}(b)-\mathcal{U}_{m,r}(b)\right]. (12.4)

Win rate measures how often a method attains the highest observed utility at an individual budget. It is a strict measure and can be sensitive to small differences between methods. Near-best rate measures how often a method remains within ϵ\epsilon of the best observed utility and is therefore less sensitive to small estimation differences. Mean regret measures the average utility lost relative to the best observed method and accounts for the magnitude of each difference.

We use ϵ=0.02\epsilon=0.02, corresponding to two percentage points of budget utility. Exact ties count as wins for every tied method, so win rates need not sum to 100%100\%. Each metric is first averaged over budgets within a setting and then averaged equally across settings. Settings with denser evaluation grids therefore receive no additional weight. Win and near-best rates are reported as percentages, while regret is reported in percentage points.

Uncertainty.

Budget evaluations within a setting share a trained policy and overlapping tasks, so individual budget points are not independent replicates. Table 2 reports descriptive point estimates, without confidence intervals or a test of differences between methods. The separate seed study below assesses training variability for two objectives in one setting; it does not quantify uncertainty for every pooled ranking.

12.2 Seed Robustness and Longer Training

The comparisons in Section 4.2 use one training seed per method and setting. To check how much of the spread between methods is training noise, we retrain Sigmoid-Gate and Linear-Mag on Qwen3.5-9B with AppWorld step budgets using two further seeds, and continue these runs from the 120120 updates of the main results to 200200 updates. Figure 7 reports their budget utility on test-normal.

After 120120 updates, the three Linear-Mag seeds differ by around ten percentage points at intermediate budgets, and the Sigmoid-Gate seeds by a few points. The broad ranking of the two methods is preserved across seeds and with longer training, with Sigmoid-Gate generally achieving higher utility at tighter and intermediate budgets. The curves become closer and can cross at the loosest budgets, where the budget is less restrictive. Training for 200200 updates improves utility at many budgets.

12.3 Resource Use on BabyAI

Budget utility measures whether a task is completed within budget, but it does not show how a policy adjusts its spending or how severely it exceeds the budget when it fails to comply. Figure 8 therefore reports mean trajectory spend and conditional overspend magnitude across BabyAI turn budgets.

Mean spend is the average number of turns used by the policy. It shows whether resource use changes with the available budget. Lower spend is not necessarily better because using additional turns may improve task success. We define conditional overspend magnitude as

Excess⁡(b)=𝔼⁡[C¯​(ζ,b)−1|C¯​(ζ,b)>1].\mathrm{Excess}(b)=\mathbb{E}\left[\bar{C}(\zeta,b)-1\;\middle|\;\bar{C}(\zeta,b)>1\right]. (12.5)

This is the expected relative excess among trajectories that exceed the budget. Compliance measures how often the policy stays within budget, while Excess⁡(b)\mathrm{Excess}(b) measures the severity of its violations. We report Excess⁡(b)\mathrm{Excess}(b) as a percentage in the figure.

Violations are generally most severe under the tightest budgets and become less severe as the budget grows.
